en: Commentary on the *Devaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, Scroll One; the preceding portion of the sūtra is missing.
The sūtra says: The World-Honored One declared: "Having few desires is the greatest peace and happiness; contentment is the highest wealth and nobility."
"One who upholds the precepts is always dignified and handsome;
one who breaks the precepts is always ugly. Commentary: This is the answer.
It answers in sequence the previous statement that "those with few desires are most at peace and happy."
Answering the first question:
parsimony constitutes "fewness," while indulgence is termed "desire."
The worldly attachments of the ignorant mind— whether slight or extensive— are swiftly destroyed;
immediately thereafter, longing arises,
and bitter affliction cuts through the heart.
The Buddha-dharma opposes worldly ways and prizes non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
Having few desires and seeking little is the supreme peace and happiness.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
One who has few desires is free from flattery and crookedness in seeking to please others;
one should cultivate even this state of having few desires as it truly is.
How much more so could they give rise to all manner of meritorious virtues?
Those who possess few desires attain nirvana;
the bliss of nirvana is the supreme among all forms of bliss.
Such supreme happiness is obtained through fewness of desires;
speaking of the cause by way of its fruit,
it is said that fewness of desires is the ultimate peace and joy.
The one who possesses the great wealth of contentment answers the second question:
Although worldly fools may attain wealth and status, their greed and seeking increase all the more, and they constantly harbor a sense of insufficiency;
the person of contentment, however, remains inactive and free from worldly affairs.
There is nothing that can be diminished or taken away;
it is always naturally in surplus,
and thus one is truly wealthy and noble.
The Sūtra says:
"A person who knows contentment is peaceful and happy even when lying upon the bare ground."
Those who lack contentment will find no satisfaction even if they dwell in heaven;
King Māndhātṛ and others are examples of this very principle.
It is further said:
"One who lacks contentment is poor despite being wealthy;
one who possesses contentment is rich despite being poor."
Therefore, it is said that contentment is the greatest wealth and nobility.
Regarding the response to the third question— “Those who maintain the precepts are always dignified and majestic”—
a person who maintains the precepts possesses pure *śīla*.
In the near term, one attains the wondrous marks that are pleasing to gods and humans;
in the distant term, one attains the majestic Dharma-body of the Three Vehicles.
Therefore, it is said that "observing the precepts results in constant majesty."
For example, King Udayana had a queen who possessed auspicious marks; she observed the one-day precept (upavāsa),
and at the end of that night, her life ended and she was reborn in the heavens with a beautiful form,
in accordance with a prior agreement with the king.
He returned below to report to the king;
finding the king's body foul-smelling, he departed back to the heavens.
This is precisely that matter.
Regarding the answer to the fourth question on how those who break the precepts are always ugly:
a person who breaks the precepts causes their sinful karma to increase and falls into the three evil realms.
They undergo the retribution of an ugly body;
if they are born among humans,
their sense faculties will be incomplete.
One's status is lowly and base, one’s physical appearance is coarse and unrefined, and people take no pleasure in seeing them.
This results from hundreds of thousands of lifetimes;
therefore, it is said that those who break the precepts are perpetually ugly and unsightly.
The Sūtra says:
The devas again requested, saying,
"Who constitutes a virtuous retinue?"
Who is the enemy of an evil mind?
What is the most grievous suffering?
And what is the supreme bliss? Commentary:
The following is the fifth section: the request for an answer.
This constitutes the request itself.
It also contains four questions.
First, one asks about virtuous kinsmen;
second, one asks about malicious enemies;
third, one asks about extreme suffering.
Regarding the first of the four questions:
"Who is a good companion?"—this is the first question.
"Companion" (眷) refers to family members.
"Belonging" refers to kinship.
Among worldly relatives, it may be that the father is not affectionate,
or the son is not filial.
Perhaps the elder brother is not compliant;
perhaps the younger brother is not respectful;
or perhaps those related internally or externally are neither benevolent nor righteous.
Their dispositions are at odds and obstructed, appearing like enemies;
though they are called kinsmen,
they are not virtuous.

If the father is compassionate and the son filial, the elder brother obedient and the younger brother respectful, and all relatives, both internal and external, treat one another with benevolence and righteousness such that their hearts are free from discord,
harmonizing like water and milk— such a family is called "virtuous."
Among those who have not yet realized the Dharma, who can be called a purely virtuous retinue?
And what constitutes an evil-minded enemy? This is the second question.
To envy the worthy and be jealous of the superior is what is termed an evil mind.
To desire to inflict harm upon one another is called enmity.
Within the Dharma that has not yet been understood, who is the enemy of the practitioner’s evil mind?
What constitutes the most grievous suffering? This is the third question.
In this world, being oppressed by killing, binding, shackling, imprisonment, encountering enemies, separation from loved ones, and illness and death is called suffering.
Within the realm of the unknown, is there further affliction and suffering that exceeds this?
"What is the foremost pleasure? This is the fourth question. [The answer is:
"In the world, the wealthy and noble ride fat horses and wear light garments;
their eyes behold beautiful women, and their ears listen to the music of strings and flutes."
Hunting and roaming in the fields, indulging in lust and wine,
and giving rein to licentious pleasure— this they call "joy.
Do you not know whether there is any joy within the Dharma that surpasses this?
The Sūtra says:
The World-Honored One declared,
"Merit is one's virtuous kinsmen."
Sin is the enemy of the evil mind;
the hells are the most grievous suffering;
non-arising is the supreme bliss. Commentary:
This is the response.
It answers the preceding four questions in sequence.
The statement that "merit constitutes a virtuous retinue" answers the first question.
Merit refers to the three virtues of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation.
Giving is of three kinds.
The first is the gift of material wealth.
The gift of fearlessness is accomplished through the wholesome root of non-attachment;
it is accomplished through the wholesome root of non-hatred.
The third is the gift of Dharma,
which is accomplished through the wholesome root of non-delusion.
There are three kinds of ethical discipline.
First is the precept of gathering others,
which refers to the three bodily [actions] and is accomplished through the wholesome root of non-attachment.
Second is the precept of not harming others,
which refers to the four verbal [abstinences] and is accomplished through the wholesome root of non-hatred.
Third is the precept of benefiting others.
This refers to the continuous arising of these two types of merit through the upholding [of the precepts],
accomplished by means of the wholesome root of non-delusion.
Cultivation is of three kinds.
First, the four dhyānas,
which are accomplished through the wholesome root of non-attachment.
The four immeasurables are accomplished by means of the wholesome root of non-hatred; the four formless attainments are likewise so accomplished.
It is accomplished through the wholesome root of non-delusion.
Furthermore, among the six perfections, the first five are also merit.
Such merit and virtue all have the ten paths of wholesome action as their nature.
If one practices the two merits of giving and ethical discipline,
in every place of rebirth, one will internally attain a superior body as a human or deva within the desire realm,
and externally attract a pure retinue through the ten wholesome paths of action.
That is to say: one’s life is not cut short;
one possesses great wealth and practices the holy life;
and one’s words are truthful and sincere.
Always using gentle speech,
one's retinue will not be estranged,
and one will skillfully reconcile disputes and litigation.
Their speech is invariably beneficial;
they are free from envy and anger,
and those with right view take them as their kinsmen.
If one cultivates the merit of meditative concentration,
one will obtain an excellent body in the form or formless realms;
these three types of merit may even lead, in the long run, to the attainment of the noble fruits of the Three Vehicles.
The meaning of the answer is as follows:
Worldly virtuous kinsmen meet for a brief moment and are parted forever;
they are difficult to assemble and easy to disperse.
One cannot guarantee its endurance for long.
It is not yet known that the three types of meritorious karma within the Dharma are truly firm and stable,
constantly supporting practitioners with manifold benefits.
Among all retinues, this is the most excellent.
Regarding the second question, "sin" refers to the enemy of an evil mind;
the destruction of the Triple Gem, the five heinous crimes, and the ten non-virtuous actions are all termed "sins."
Due to these transgressions,
they cause sentient beings to revolve and fall into the three miserable realms,
suffering for long kalpas.
The intent of this reply is as follows: In the world, even a malicious mind that harms but a single person is still called an enemy;
how much more so, then, regarding the karmic offenses within the Dharma?
Since it can harm many lifetimes,
is it not a great enemy? Therefore,
it is said that sin is the enemy of the evil mind.
"The most intense suffering of the hells" answers the third question.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *naraka*;
the older transliteration "niraya" is an error.
In the language of Tang, it is called "the place of no joy.
However, since the place of no joy is precisely hell,
and because it mostly lies beneath the earth, it is called "hell" (dìyù).
There are three hot hells, two cold hells, and three peripheral hells.
There are eight hot hells:
the first is Saṃjīva (Reviving).
Second, Kālasūtra (Black Rope);
third, Saṃghāta (Crushing);
fourth, Raurava (Crying Out).
The five Great Crying Hells,
the sixth, the Heating Hell,
and the seventh, the Greatly Heating Hell.
The eight hells of immediate retribution.
These eight are situated beneath Jambudvīpa,
stacked one upon another.
The first two have predominant functions;
the next three have minor functions;
the final three have no predominant functions.
However, these eight constitute the bases;
each one has sixteen gardens,
with four on each side.
The four sides together total sixteen;
including the original [central] one, they constitute seventeen.
Eight sets of seventeen amount to one hundred and thirty-six locations.
Within these, the sinners undergo the suffering of burning heat.
There are likewise eight cold hells:
the first is Arbuda.
Driven by the suffering of cold, flesh-generating cells arise;
in the second, Arbuda,
the entire body becomes covered in blisters due to being blown upon by cold winds.
Third, *aṭṭha*.
Because the lips cannot move and only the tongue can move,
this sound is produced.
The four *āpāpa* sounds are produced because the tongue cannot move and only the lips can;
thus, this sound is made.
Fifth, *huhu*: because the lips and tongue cannot move, one produces this sound by vibrating the breath.
Sixth, *utpala*.
This is a blue lotus flower.
The petals of this flower are fine;
because the flesh is thin and split, it resembles the opening of this flower.
Seventh is Padma; this refers to the red lotus.
Because the flesh splits wide open like the petals of this flower, it is so named.
Eight are *puṇḍarīkas*. These are white lotuses;
because their bones split open like the blossoming of these flowers, they are so named.
The first two receive their names from the characteristic of the body;
the next three receive their names from the characteristic of sound;
and the final three receive their names from the characteristic of sores.
Furthermore, among these, the first two are conscious cries;
the next three are unconscious cries;
and the final three are not cries at all.
These eight are situated between the four continents;
they rest upon the base of the Cakravāḍa Mountains,
dwelling with their hearts turned upward.
Within it, the sinners undergo the suffering of cold and freezing.
There are three peripheral hells:
first, the mountain clefts.
Second, between two waters;
third, in a wilderness—
receiving these as the retributions for distinct karmic actions.
"Cold and heat are experienced in combination.
The intent of this response is as follows:

although there are the sufferings of humans—such as being killed, bound, shackled, encountering enemies, being separated from loved ones, illness, and death—as well as the sufferings of animals and hungry ghosts.
Compared to the hells, [the former] does not equal even one hundredth part of it;
indeed, it does not equal even one part in ten million nayutas.
Therefore, it is said that the suffering of the hells is the most extreme.
Regarding "the unarisen is the supreme bliss," this answers the fourth question.
The essence of nirvāṇa is called "the unarisen" (anutpāda);
it is so named because it is unarisen.
It is ultimately non-extinguishing;
the sage realizes this and enters the tranquil nirvana.
It is eternally abiding and secure;
therefore, it is "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
This is the intended meaning of the answer.
The pleasures of the world reach their ultimate limit in suffering;
how can they compare to the eternal bliss of Nirvana, which is free from suffering?
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
That which is high must fall;
that which is permanent must end;
that which is joined must separate.
"What is pleasant must end in suffering.
This verse clarifies that the delusive pleasures of birth and death, when their intensity reaches its peak, inevitably turn into suffering.
It further states:
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are subject to the law of arising and ceasing.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, nirvana is bliss.
This verse clarifies that nirvāṇa is free from suffering and is ultimately eternal bliss; therefore,
it is said to be the supreme bliss of non-arising.
The Sūtra says:
The devas again requested, saying:
"What is that craving which is inappropriate?"
What is undesirable? What is the most feverish illness?
Who is the great physician? The commentary states:
The following is the sixth section, the request for an answer.
This constitutes the initial request,
which likewise contains four questions.
First, asking what is pleasant but inappropriate;
second, asking what is appropriate but unpleasant;
third, asking about the fever of extreme passion.
The four questions concern the great physician.
First, what is beloved but unsuitable? Second, what is suitable but not beloved? These are the first and second questions.
For instance, sweet rice mixed with poison, though it is something one desires, [is unsuitable].
Furthermore, it harms the body and endangers life;
therefore, one should not eat it.
It is also like a potent medicine that is bitter to the taste and thus not something one desires.
Yet it is beneficial for the illness and should be taken accordingly.
It is also like flattering words that accord with one's desires; though they may be beloved, [they are not to be accepted].
This will cause harm to one's conduct;
it is not appropriate to listen to such things.
Though loyal words may be harsh to the ear and contrary to what one desires to hear, they must still be accepted.
It is beneficial for practice;
you should listen to it.
Yet, among the teachings, you do not yet know which ones are what your heart truly loves.
Yet it is not suitable for the body.
What is it that is suitable for the body but is not loved by sentient beings?
"What is the 'extremely feverish disease'?"—this is the third question.
The *kāmalā* disease is commonly referred to in the world as a "feverish disease";
one who encounters this illness is certain to die.
The worldly physicians fold their hands in helplessness, not knowing whether within the Dharma there might be any illness even more extreme than this feverish disease.
Who is the Great Physician? This is the fourth question.
"Liáng" means "good. "Yī" means "intention.
It refers to being skilled at identifying the source of a disease.
If the medicinal properties of the sandalwood are applied,
the patient will surely recover; thus,
he is called a skilled physician.
A skilled physician possesses four qualities:
first, knowledge of the disease;
second, knowledge of the cause of the disease.
Third, knowing the illness has been cured;
fourth, knowing that once cured, it will not recur.
Within the teachings I have not yet known, is there perhaps a skilled physician whose great excellence is equal to that of this physician?
The Sūtra says:
The World-Honored One declared,
"All sensual desires and cravings are improper."
It is said that what is unloved should be explained;
craving is a most feverish disease, and the Buddha is the Great Physician. Commentary:
This is the answer.
It answers the preceding four questions in sequence.
The statement that "all sensual desires are unsuitable" answers the first question.
The various desires refer to the five objects of desire—lovely forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
They are called "desires" because they give rise to the mind of desire and are thus taken as objects of grasping.
As the Sūtra says:
The five desires deceive people;
they are like licking a knife coated with honey—the tongue is wounded.
They are also like roasting a scab: though there is a slight pleasure at first, [it leads to harm].
Thereafter comes great suffering.
It is like holding a torch against the wind; if one does not let go, it will surely burn one's hand.
It is like a king who, through greed for sensual pleasures, ultimately loses his throne.
The Rishi Priyarūpa fell from the sky into the forest;
the Bhikṣu smelled his fragrance and was rebuked by the river deity;
the Śrāmaṇera tasted its flavor and threw himself into the pond to become a dragon.
Rāvaṇa lost his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) because he was stained by sensory contact.

Furthermore, these five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) currently entail the experience of three kinds of suffering: namely, the suffering of exertion (*pariśrama*) incurred at the time of seeking them; [the suffering of possession; and the suffering of change].
Missing the proper time gives rise to the suffering of fear;
losing the proper time gives rise to the suffering of burning affliction.
Furthermore, one pursues the five sensual desires through unrighteous means.
Furthermore, they will fall again into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, suffering for a long time. Subsequently,
even if born among humans or devas, they will experience the miseries of poverty,
affliction, and the pain of separation from loved ones.
Enmity increases suffering;
such sufferings as these all arise from the causal conditions of attachment to the five desires.
Thus we know that although the five desires are what the deluded minds of ordinary people love, [they are ultimately harmful].
However, this is utterly inappropriate for a practitioner;
therefore, it is said that "all sensual desires are inappropriate.
To answer the second question, it is stated that "liberation is appropriate, not desire."
Nirvāṇa is unconditioned and its essence is free from all bonds;
therefore, it is called liberation.
Those who realize liberation are forever separated from birth and death.
It is eternally abiding and profoundly serene;
as such, it is most appropriate for those who practice by means of the provisions for liberation.
Yet, it is something that the deluded minds of ordinary people do not cherish.
Therefore, it is said that liberation should not be craved.
Thus, a sutra states:
"An ordinary person would rather take pleasure in the body of a leper or a jackal."
They do not delight in nirvāṇa;
for while the jackal still possesses eyes, ears, and a mind,
these are absent in nirvāṇa.
Regarding the answer to the third question, "Greed is a fever of extreme intensity":
greed is the latent tendency of greed (*rāgānuśaya*);
its substance pervades the three realms.
Pervasively obstructing the five inquiries,
it functions simultaneously with the six consciousnesses and is equally defiled by the six sense objects.
The feet and soles of birth and death are the root source of suffering and affliction;
how could the fevers of the world compare to this?
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
The fire of desire blazes fiercely within the sacrificial altar of the heavens;
is not craving indeed a most feverish illness?
Even now, one is scorched by its flames.
In a future life, how could one possibly avoid the boiling cauldrons?
Therefore, it is said that greed is the fever of extreme heat.
This is the Buddha’s response to the fourth question, as he is the Great Physician.
The Tathāgata’s five eyes possess the inner clarity of the six supernormal powers and the outer brilliance that vertically observes the three periods of time.
Looking transversely across the ten directions,
from the sources of physical and mental illness to the medicinal methods for their removal, all are clearly illuminated as if before one's eyes; thus,
the establishment of teachings to accommodate various capacities is entirely in accordance with the individual's root-nature.
Administering medicine according to the specific ailment ensures that no one fails to benefit;
therefore, the Buddha is the supreme and most excellent physician.
Thus it is said in the Āgama Sūtras.
The Buddha possesses four types of knowledge:
first, knowing suffering;
second, knowing the cause of suffering.
Third, he knows the cessation of suffering;
fourth, he knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Therefore, he is called a skilled physician.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"Though treated by worldly physicians,
even when cured, the illness arises again."
That which has been treated by the Tathāgata will never again arise;
therefore, it is said that the Buddha is the Great Physician.
The Sūtra says:
The deva asked again:
"Who is able to cover the world?
By whom is the world possessed?"
"Who causes one to abandon kinsmen and friends?
Who again obstructs rebirth in heaven? Commentary:
This concludes the seventh request for an answer.
This is the initial request.
There are also four questions.
The first question conceals the world.
Second, the question on bewitching the world;
third, the question on abandoning friends;
fourth, the question on obstructing the heavens.
"Who is able to shroud the world?"—this is the first question.
"Shrouding" means to obstruct or conceal;
it refers to the eye of the world being shrouded by the darkness of blindness.
Not seeing forms or images,
and not yet knowing what further things within the Dharma obscure the world,
they do not recognize the underlying principles.
"By whom in the world are people possessed?"— this is the second question.
Just as worldly ghosts and spirits possess people and cause them to become deluded,
making them either weep or rejoice.
"Among the unknown phenomena, what further thing is there that can enchant the world and cause it to become deluded?
Who causes one to abandon one's kinsmen?"— this is the third question.
When friendships are formed through close and frequent association, they become true kin and friends;
however, if they are based on wealth,
they grow distant once that wealth is exhausted.
If one relies on the influence of power,
that relationship will be obstructed once the power wanes;
this is exemplified by the tragic end of Zhang and Chen, and the final breach between Xiao and Zhu.
Among those who have not yet realized the Dharma, who causes sentient beings to abandon their kinsmen and friends?
And who further obstructs those destined for rebirth in heaven? This is the fourth question.
As for the superior retribution of the heavens, all beings there experience happiness.
By what obstacle is one prevented from attaining rebirth in the higher realms?
The Sūtra says:
The World-Honored One replied, "Ignorance shrouds the world."
The world is deluded by ignorance; through stinginess and greed, they abandon their kin and friends.
Attachment acts as an obstacle to rebirth in the heavens. Commentary:
This is the answer.
It answers the preceding four questions in sequence.
The statement "the world is shrouded by ignorance" answers the first question.
Lacking the wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path,
or lacking the wisdom regarding the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional,
is called "lack of wisdom."
Lack of wisdom is precisely the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*).
Because of this lack of wisdom,
one does not know the causes that accumulate for the fruit of suffering within birth and death.
They do not know that the cause of the path to liberation is the cessation of results;
they do not know the single characteristic of the true truth (paramārtha-satya), which is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta);
and they do not know the causes and effects of the three periods of time according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The intent of this response is as follows:
in the world, blindness and darkness merely shroud the physical eye;
it is only the lack of wisdom that can shroud the worldly eye of insight (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
Therefore, it is said that "ignorance shrouds the world.
Those in the world who are bewitched by delusion answer the second question;
"delusion" (*moha*) is another name for "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
Due to being possessed by delusion,
one perceives permanence in the impermanent and perceives a self in what is non-self.
To perceive purity in the impure and to perceive pleasure in suffering—
all such modes of understanding and resolve are entirely inverted.
Such inversions arise from ignorance;
therefore, it is said that "the world is possessed by delusion.
Regarding the third question, [the Buddha] answered that stinginess and greed cause one to abandon friends and kin.
Avarice (mātsarya) is stinginess regarding one's own possessions;
greed (lobha) is the desire for the wealth of others,
as stated in the Vinaya.
There was a bhikṣu practicing meditative concentration by the side of a pond.
A nāga of the pond, out of reverence for his virtue, coiled its body around him.
The bhikṣu felt aversion in his heart and wished for the nāga to depart.
Using skillful means, he spoke a verse to request the pearl, saying:
"The radiant maṇi jewel adorns the body with its necklace."
"If one can bestow [this] upon me,
that person is called a true kinsman.
Thus spoke the nāga of the pond, who, being stingy and miserly, replied with this verse.
"I cherish this mani-jewel;
having encountered you, O bhikṣu,
I shall never bestow it upon you."
"Let it be as you wish; we shall not associate with you.
On account of this matter, the Buddha further spoke a verse, saying:
"One who is full of greed is loathed by others."
The mendicant repeatedly asked his friend for the dragon's pearl;
once it was gone, he never returned.
Thus we know that stinginess and greed can cause one to abandon friends and relatives.
Furthermore, due to greed, one desires only the wealth of others;
due to stinginess, one does not practice giving.
In whatever place they are born, they will be impoverished and destitute;
they will have no father and no mother,
and no wife and no children.
There are no virtuous friends and no close companions; therefore,
it is said that stinginess and greed cause one to abandon close friends.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states that there are five kinds of stinginess:
first, stinginess regarding giving;
second, stinginess regarding families.
Third is stinginess regarding places;
fourth is stinginess regarding praise;
fifth is stinginess regarding the Dharma.
These five types of stinginess all cause one to abandon friends and relatives.
Regarding the answer to the fourth question concerning those obstructed by attachment from being born in heaven—
"heaven" refers to the twenty-eight heavens.
In all cases, one must cultivate weariness with the lower realms to attain birth in the higher realms;
if one is stained by attachment to the lower stages,
one cannot be born in the higher ones.
If one is stained by and attached to the five desires among humans,
indulging in them with heedlessness and refusing to feel weary of them or seek renunciation,
one will not attain rebirth in the six heavens of the desire realm.
As explained at length in the sūtra:
the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda, weary of Sundarī and longing for the celestial maidens,
only then began to observe the precepts with the aspiration to be reborn in heaven.
If one becomes attached to the five desires of the six heavens,
one will not attain rebirth among the gods of the Form Realm;
if one becomes attached to the karmic rewards of the Form Realm, [one will likewise fail to transcend it].
One cannot be reborn in the formless heavens;
therefore, it is said that attachment is an obstacle to birth in the heavens.
Furthermore, the noble ones of the three vehicles are called "pure heavens."
If one is stained by and attached to the tainted retributions of the twenty-eight heavens within the three realms,
one will not be able to enter the noble path of the Three Vehicles;
this is also called the obstacle of attachment that prevents rebirth in heaven.
The Sūtra says:
The deva further requested, saying,
"Who is it that is not burned by fire?"
Even the wind cannot shatter it;
who is not rotted by water?
It is able to float and support the world.
Who is able to oppose the king's enemies with such valor as to withstand them,
whether they be humans or non-humans?
"Regarding that which comes to invade and seize," the commentary states:
this is the eighth request for an answer below;
this constitutes the preliminary request.
There are two intentions behind these questions:
first, to ask who is free from the seven calamities;
second, to ask who possesses the one capability.
Regarding the seven perils:
first, the peril of fire;
second, the peril of wind.
1. The difficulty of the three waters;
2. The difficulty of the four kings;
3. The difficulty of bandits.
The sixth is the difficulty of humans;
the seventh is the difficulty of ghosts.
Fire poses the difficulty of burning and scorching; wind poses the difficulty of blowing and shattering.
For water, the difficulty lies in drowning and scalding;
for a king, the difficulty lies in his sovereign power;
for a bandit, the difficulty lies in plundering and killing.
Human beings find it difficult to avoid being harmed by others;
ghosts find it difficult to avoid being possessed by malevolent spirits.
Most people in the world cannot escape these seven kinds of calamities.
Among those who have not yet realized the Dharma, who can escape these seven kinds of calamities?
The scriptural text is easy to understand.
First, "one who is capable" refers to one who is able to float and support the world.
There are two kinds of worlds:
first, the receptacle world, which is the environment resulting from collective karma.
Second is the world of sentient beings, which refers to their primary retribution (*vipāka*).
Just as the water-circle in the world can support and sustain the earth-circle and the various classes of sentient beings, so it is here.
Among those who do not yet know the Dharma, who is able to support these two worlds?
This is due to water having two functions:
first, it can cause things to decompose.
Second, because it can support the earth.
Question: Following the discussion on the water’s power to soften, one now asks about its power to float and support.
The Sūtra says:
The World-Honored One said:
"Merit cannot be burned by fire,
nor can it be shattered by wind."
Merit cannot be rotted by water;
it can support and sustain the world.
Merit can provide [protection] against kings and thieves.
Bravely contending against enemies,
one shall not be invaded or plundered by humans or non-humans. Commentary states:
This is the answer.
It answers the first two questions.
"Merit" refers to the three kinds of merit: those consisting of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation.
As explained previously in the section on virtuous associates,
the answer regarding the absence of the seven calamities means that whenever one encounters these seven kinds of disasters, [one is protected].
One creates the causes for the ten evil deeds;
having already cultivated the three kinds of merit,
how could one possibly suffer the seven kinds of calamities?
Question:
It may be permissible to resist bandits who act unrighteously;
however, persons and the law belong to the king.
"How can one resist the enemy? Answer:
"It is like Zhou Wu resisting the tyrannical King Zhou of Yin."
Although these are royal officials,
they may still oppose one another;
furthermore, "king" is a general term.
Furthermore, those who style themselves as subjects and vassals,
and those who carry the king’s commands, are likewise called "kings.
Thus, both these kings and their ministers commit acts of violence and cruel oppression.
Those who act unrighteously are like thieves;
one may even resist them.
As it is said in the sutras:
There was a king who reprimanded a minister and ordered him to inventory the family's property.
The minister then proceeded to inventory the items he had used for the cultivation of merit.
The king, filled with anger, rebuked him, saying:
"The goods for which merit was previously cultivated are now all seen to be gone;
why do you not record the items currently present in your home?
The minister replied to the king:
Wealth already expended on merit belongs to the subjects;
the property currently present in the household originally belongs to the five families and is not possessed by the minister alone.
For this reason, it was not recorded.
King Xuan’s mind opened to awakening,
and he subsequently also cultivated merit.
Therefore, it is known that this merit cannot be taken away by others.
The answer is: there is one who possesses the intention [to do so], which is said to be due to three kinds of merit.
One brings about the sublime primary retribution of gods and humans,
and simultaneously brings about the various secondary fruits of the environment, such as dwellings and material resources;
therefore, it is said that merit can support and sustain the world.
Question:
Confucius, Laozi, and others say that from the Dao, the One is produced.
From one, two is produced;
from two, three is produced;
from three, the myriad things are produced.
The Way refers to emptiness and penetration.
"One" refers to the primal qi;
"two" refers to yin and yang.
The "three" refers to heaven, earth, and humanity.
"The myriad things" refers to animals, plants, grasses, trees, and so forth.
It is further stated:
The roundness of the human head resembles heaven;
the squareness of the feet resembles earth.
One is formed as a human being by responding to the vital essence of heaven and earth.
According to this, it is the external receptacle world that is able to support the sentient world;
how could it be that the internal merit of sentient beings is able to support the external receptacle world of water?
Answer: What Confucius and Laozi speak of is that Heaven and Earth give birth to humans; what the Buddhist school elucidates is that humans give rise to Heaven and Earth.
This means that through the collective karmic power of sentient beings, they externally perceive the objective realm, wherein Heaven and Earth serve as the environmental support (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Whether regarding formation or destruction, as explained in detail elsewhere,
the Sūtra says:
"All that is produced within the three realms is but the one mind."
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"The external is established by means of the internal.
This implies that Confucius and Laozi merely observed the sequential order of external phenomena.
This means that while heaven and earth give birth to humans,
the Tathāgata, through his profound knowledge of the internal causes and effects of the body,
teaches that humans give birth to heaven and earth.
The relative depth and shallowness of the three teachings can be understood by observing this.
The Sūtra says:
The Deva further requested, saying:
I still have doubts;
may the Buddha sever them for me:
concerning this life and future lives.
"Who is it that utterly deceives himself? The commentary states:
This is the ninth request for an answer;
herein, the request is first made.
The first half of the verse sets forth the inquiry, while the second half poses the actual question.
The intent of this introductory inquiry is as follows:
I have received your extensive reply,
which has already resolved my many points of stagnation;
yet my humble mind remains largely deluded, and there are still lingering doubts.
I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will sever this for me.
In the midst of the formal inquiry, it says:
"The present life" refers to the current existence.
"Later generations" refers to the future;
it means proceeding from the present body to a subsequent body.
Question:
Conditioned phenomena are impermanent, neither coming nor going,
and furthermore lack a sovereign master;
who then can be said to go?
Answer: The preceding perishes and the succeeding arises; it is neither eternal nor discontinuous.
Because the cause invites the fruit and the succession continues, we conventionally speak of "going" and "coming."
For example, it is like taking a lamp from here to there;
although it perishes moment by moment, we conventionally speak of its "going" and "coming. Question:
The cycle of cause and effect throughout the three periods of time is complete and circular; why,
then, do you specifically inquire about the present and the future,
rather than asking about the past?
Answer: The previous matter has already been concluded;
there is no need for further questioning.
Since the subsequent body has not yet been received, one must request it;
this is like the gods prostrating before a white-boned hungry ghost (preta) or whipping a corpse.
Since most matters already known are understood by oneself,
they are not asked about. The intent of this question is as follows:
Those who deceive in the world merely wish to harm others;
do they not know that within the Dharma there is something even more self-destructive and utterly deceptive than this?
The Sūtra says:
The World-Honored One said,
"If one possesses abundant wealth and treasures..."
Yet they do not cultivate merit for this life or for lives to come;
they utterly deceive themselves. It is said:
This is the answer. "Treasures" (zhen) refers to the eight precious substances, such as gold and silver;
"wealth" (cai) refers to items such as money and silk.
The people of the world are deluded and ignorant;
they believe themselves to be eternal and do not recognize the law of cause and effect.
Though they accumulate vast wealth and treasures,
they lack the intention to practice generosity toward those who are fields of compassion,
and they lack the intent to offer worship to those who are fields of reverence.
Suddenly their lives come to an end, and with not a single merit to support them,
they fall by the wheel of karma into the three miserable realms, suffering for a long time.
While others enjoy wealth and precious treasures,
one possesses not even a fragment of goodness;
is this not a cause for self-reproach?
Therefore it is said: "If one possesses abundant wealth and treasures yet is unable to cultivate merit, they utterly deceive themselves as they pass from this life to the next.
Furthermore, as a sutra states: "To begrudge wealth and fail to practice giving [is a great folly]."
Accumulating wealth while fearing others will know of it,
one departs empty-handed after casting off the body;
one undergoes hunger among the hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, as a sutra says:
"All kinsmen and relatives are separated;
only karma does not abandon one."
Good and evil follow one at all times throughout future lives.
In this regard, one should cite the person who has three wives as an analogy, and one should also cite the person who has three sons as an analogy.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"It would be better to cut off one's own flesh and eat it than to be unwilling to give away wealth in charity to seek merit in future lives."
This person shall fall into the sufferings of the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth.
The Sūtra says:
"At that time, those devas, having heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preach this sūtra... [The Commentary] states:
Below this is the third section, the "Section on Receiving and Practicing According to the Teaching," which constitutes the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) and has three parts:
first, hearing the Dharma;
second, expressing reverence.
Third is returning from concealment;
this refers to hearing the Dharma.
As the Sūtra says:
Rejoicing and leaping for joy, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
They prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet. [The Commentary] states:
This is an expression of reverence.
Having heard the sublime Dharma,
one cannot help but joyfully express reverence for its virtue.
Therefore, he again praised the ritual.
The Sūtra says:
"At that moment before the Buddha, he suddenly vanished. The Commentary states:
This is my return from seclusion.
I have come to consult you regarding my doubts;
I have already received your analysis of my obscurities, and what I harbored in my mind has now been fulfilled.
Therefore, Yin returned to the palace.
*Tianqingwen jing shu*, one fascicle.
